Exmoor: Where the Moor Plunges into the Sea

Exmoor National Park straddles the Devon-Somerset border, and its defining feature is the point where high, open moorland meets the Bristol Channel coast in England's highest sea cliffs. At 267 square miles, Exmoor is smaller and quieter than its neighbour Dartmoor, but many riders prefer it — the combination of moorland roads, spectacular coastal scenery, deep wooded combes, and charming villages creates a motorcycle touring experience that's hard to beat anywhere in southern England.

The Coastal Roads

Exmoor's coast is sensational. The A39 from Minehead to Lynmouth follows the coast with dramatic views across the Bristol Channel to Wales. Porlock Hill is one of England's most famous roads — the old toll road drops at an astonishing 1-in-4 gradient through hairpin bends canopied by ancient trees. The newer A39 bypass is still steep but more forgiving. Either way, the descent into the Vale of Porlock is thrilling.

Lynton and Lynmouth

Lynton and Lynmouth are twin villages connected by a Victorian cliff railway. Lynmouth sits at the foot of towering cliffs where the East Lyn River meets the sea. The village was devastated by a flood in 1952 but has been beautifully rebuilt. Lynton perches on the cliff top above, with panoramic views along the coast. The Valley of Rocks, just west of Lynton, is one of Exmoor's most dramatic landscapes — wild goats graze among weathered rock formations above the sea.

The Moorland Interior

Exmoor's interior is a landscape of purple heather, wild ponies, and red deer — Exmoor supports England's largest wild red deer herd. The road from Simonsbath to Exford crosses the high moor with sweeping views. Dunkery Beacon, at 519 metres, is the highest point in Somerset — the view from the summit encompasses the Brecon Beacons, Dartmoor, and the Quantock Hills.

  • Simonsbath — Remote moorland village at the heart of the former Royal Forest, excellent walking base
  • Exford — Pretty village on the River Exe, traditional hunting centre, good pub
  • Winsford — Thatched cottages, a packhorse bridge, and the Royal Oak pub
  • Dulverton — Southern gateway to Exmoor, independent shops, and riverside walks
  • Dunster — Medieval village with a castle, yarn market, and cobbled streets
Exmoor is England's forgotten national park. While the crowds head to the Lake District and Dartmoor, Exmoor quietly offers some of the finest riding in the country — dramatic coast, wild moors, and roads empty enough to make you feel like the only person in the world.

Best Riding Roads

Beyond the coast road, seek out these gems:

  • Porlock Hill — The old toll road with 1-in-4 gradients and hairpin bends through oak woodland
  • A396 Exe Valley — Follows the River Exe through deep wooded valleys from Dunster to Tiverton
  • B3223 Simonsbath to Lynton — High moorland crossing with expansive views
  • B3224 Exford to Wheddon Cross — Quintessential Exmoor moorland road
  • Countisbury Hill — Dramatic climb from Lynmouth with 1-in-4 gradients and cliff-edge views

Food and Local Character

Exmoor's food scene revolves around local produce. Exmoor venison and Ruby Red beef are specialities. The Rising Sun in Lynmouth and the Royal Oak at Winsford serve outstanding food in atmospheric settings. Porlock has several excellent tearooms. Local cider from the Somerset orchards is the traditional drink — seek out farmhouse scrumpy for the authentic experience.

Practical Information

Exmoor is accessed via the M5 motorway to Taunton or Bridgwater, then A-roads west into the park. From London, allow 3.5 hours; from Bristol, 90 minutes; from Exeter, an hour. Fuel is available in Minehead, Dulverton, South Molton, and Barnstaple — top up before heading onto the moor. Accommodation ranges from country house hotels to campsites and B&Bs. Roads can be narrow with steep gradients and blind bends — ride within your limits, especially on the coastal hills. Watch for Exmoor ponies and red deer on unfenced roads. Best months: May to October, with August-September being ideal for heather on the moors. Exmoor is also designated as an International Dark Sky Reserve — stay overnight and you'll see stars like nowhere else in southern England.

faq.q: What is Porlock Hill like on a motorcycle?
faq.a: Porlock Hill is one of England's most famous roads. The old toll road drops at an astonishing 1-in-4 gradient through hairpin bends canopied by ancient trees, while the newer A39 bypass is still steep but more forgiving. Either way, the descent into the Vale of Porlock is thrilling. Countisbury Hill near Lynmouth offers a similar 1-in-4 challenge with cliff-edge views.

faq.q: Will I see wildlife on Exmoor?
faq.a: Very likely. Exmoor's interior is a landscape of purple heather, wild ponies and red deer, and the park supports England's largest wild red deer herd. Watch for Exmoor ponies and red deer on unfenced roads, as they can step out without warning. Ride within your limits, especially on the steep coastal hills.

faq.q: Where should I eat and drink on Exmoor?
faq.a: Exmoor's food revolves around local produce, with Exmoor venison and Ruby Red beef as specialities. The Rising Sun in Lynmouth and the Royal Oak at Winsford serve outstanding food in atmospheric settings, and Porlock has several excellent tearooms. Local farmhouse cider, or scrumpy, from the Somerset orchards is the authentic drink.

faq.q: How do I get to Exmoor?
faq.a: Exmoor is accessed via the M5 motorway to Taunton or Bridgwater, then A-roads west into the park. Allow 3.5 hours from London, 90 minutes from Bristol and an hour from Exeter. Fuel is available in Minehead, Dulverton, South Molton and Barnstaple, so top up before heading onto the moor where stations are scarce.

Yes. Exmoor is designated as an International Dark Sky Reserve, so if you stay overnight you will see stars like nowhere else in southern England. The best months to visit are May to October, with August and September ideal for the heather on the moors. Combine a day's riding with an evening under exceptionally dark skies.
